title: Coding Intros
text:
Preface
The purpose of this tutorial is to introduce the programming languages R and Python that are used during the lectures, in problem sets, and in the tutorials. The tutorial consists of two parallel parts:

Part I: Introduction to R
Part II: Introduction to Python

Both parts have the same structure: each chapter of the R part has a counterpart in the Python part that covers the same topics with the same examples and exercises. So you can work through the part of your preferred language, or compare how the same task is done in both languages.

Downloads

R is free of charge and can be downloaded from https://cran.r-project.org/
Python is free of charge and can be downloaded from https://www.python.org/downloads/
The IDE Positron for R and Python is also free of charge and can be downloaded from
https://positron.posit.co/download.html



On Using LLMs
Of course, you can also ask large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT or Claude. But: Don’t fool yourself! Getting an answer from an LLM is not the same as learning and understanding.

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
1.1 Positron for the First Time
I highly recommend to install Positron. For installation just follow the instructions onhttps://positron.posit.co/download.html
When you open Positron, its window is typically split into the following areas:
Some other terms that will be useful:
crumbs: 1  The First Steps in R

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
The editor (center) showing your script file, which is an ordinary text file with suffix .R. For instance, yourFavoritFileName.R. This file contains your code.
The Session pane (right) showing all objects (variables) we have defined in the environment.
The Plots and Help panes (right) showing plots and help files.
The Console (bottom), which allows you to type commands and display results.
The Explorer (left) showing the files in your current project folder.



Working directory: The file-directory you are working in. Useful commands: with getwd() you get the location of your current working directory and setwd() allows you to set a new location for it. This is very useful when you would like to load or save several files. You can just set your working directory globally and all files can be loaded or will be saved into this directory.
Workspace: This is a hidden file (stored in the working directory), where all objects you use (e.g., data, matrices, vectors, variables, functions, etc.) are stored. Useful commands: ls() shows all elements in our current workspace and rm(list=ls()) deletes all elements in our current workspace. It is also possible to remove only some objects with rm(object1, object2).
crumbs: 1  The First Steps in R

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
1.2 Simple Calculations
We start with a very basic calculation. Let’s type 1+1 into the console window and press enter. We get

 1+1 # first calculation

[1] 2


i.e. the result of the calculation is returned.
Note that everything that is written after the #-sign is ignored by R, which is very useful to comment your code. The second window above, starting with ##, shows the output.
Let’s consider a second calculation

1+2+3+ # second calculation

Error: <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
1: 1+2+3+ # second calculation
   ^


This calculation ended with an error. The reason is that the command can only processed if entered correctly.

1+2+3+4 # second calculation

[1] 10


A similar thing happens when parentheses are not closed.

 2*(2+3

Error: <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
1:  2*(2+3
   ^


It will be helpful to use a script file, such as yourFavoritFileName.R, to store your R commands. Otherwise, you would have to type your code again when an error occurred. You can send single lines or marked regions of your R-code to the console by pressing the keys STRG+ENTER.
crumbs: 1  The First Steps in R

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
1.3 Assigments and Matrix Algebra
The assignment operator will be your most often used tool. Here is an example where a scalar variable is created:

x <- 9
x

[1] 9

x+1

[1] 10


Note: The <- assignment operator is an unusual syntax that you do not find in other programming languages. In many cases you can alternatively use the = operator. Typical R style uses the <- assignment operator due to some more in depth-differences and compatibility with older version of R. More on R style recommendations can be found in the tidyverse style guide. In simple settings, alternatives to <- are

x = 9
x

[1] 9


or even

4 -> y # possible but unusal
y

[1] 4


We consider now a vector, an object you will use frequently:

z <- c(1,3,5,6)
z

[1] 1 3 5 6


As discussed, ls() states the content of the workspace, whereas rm(list =ls()) deletes the workspace.

ls()

[1] "x" "y" "z"

rm(list=ls())
ls()

character(0)


In the next step we will consider some vector multiplication. There are three different ways to multiply a vector, namely element by element, using the inner product, or using the outer product. Element by element gives you a vector of the same dimension.

z <- c(1,3,5,6)
z*z                #multiplication element by element

[1]  1  9 25 36


The function t() gives the transpose of a vector (or matrix). It is therefore tempting to calculate the inner product as

t(z)*z                #multiplication inner product

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    9   25   36


but this does not give the desired answer. Insead, you have to use

z <- c(1,3,5,6)
t(z)%*%z                #multiplication inner product

     [,1]
[1,]   71


Note that R stores zTz as a matrix.

class(t(z)%*%z)

[1] "matrix" "array" 

class(z)

[1] "numeric"


Finally, we have the outer product that gives us a matrix

z <- c(1,3,5,6)
z%*%t(z)                #multiplication outer product

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    3    5    6
[2,]    3    9   15   18
[3,]    5   15   25   30
[4,]    6   18   30   36


In general, be very careful with %*% versus *. They are often both feasible, but yield different results!
You can also multiply a vector with a scalar:

z*4

[1]  4 12 20 24


A strength of R is that operations can be conducted for each element of the vector in one statement

z^2

[1]  1  9 25 36

log(z)

[1] 0.000000 1.098612 1.609438 1.791759

(z-mean(z))/sd(z)

[1] -1.2402159 -0.3382407  0.5637345  1.0147221


So far, we have seen the function c() that can be used to combine objects. All function calls use the same general notation: a function name is always followed by round parentheses. Sometimes, the parentheses include arguments, such as

z <- seq(from = 1, to = 5, by = 1)
z

[1] 1 2 3 4 5


With square brackets you can access particular elements, such as

z[1:3]                  #refer to particular elements

[1] 1 2 3


We will next define a matrix and perform matrix-vector multiplication.

M <- matrix(data=1:9, nrow=3, ncol=3)    # define matrix M
M

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    4    7
[2,]    2    5    8
[3,]    3    6    9

dim(M)                                  # dimension of M

[1] 3 3

dim(z)                                  # dimension of z - does not work because z is not a matrix

NULL

length(z)                               # number of elements of z

[1] 5


Element-by-element multiplication for M is given by

M * M

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1   16   49
[2,]    4   25   64
[3,]    9   36   81


Standard matrix multiplication is again done using %*% such as

M %*% M

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   30   66  102
[2,]   36   81  126
[3,]   42   96  150



t(M) %*% M

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   14   32   50
[2,]   32   77  122
[3,]   50  122  194


If matrices and vectors have suitable dimensions, you can multiply them as follows:

M %*% z[1:3]

     [,1]
[1,]   30
[2,]   36
[3,]   42


Similar to before, with square brackets you can excess particular elements, such as

M[,3]                 # state the third column of M

[1] 7 8 9

M[3,3]                # state element in the third column and third row of M

[1] 9


Here are some more examples:

M[,1]                 # first column of M
M[3,3]                # element in the third column and third row of M
z[c(1,4)]             # first and fourth element of z

Logical statements are also very useful. For example, if you want to know which elements in the first column of matrix M are strictly greater than 2:

# See which elements:
M[,1]>2

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE

# and extract the elements
M[M[,1]>2,1]

[1] 3


Note: Logical operations return so-called boolean objects, i.e., either a TRUE or a FALSE. For instance, if we ask R whether 1>2 we get the answer FALSE.

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
1.4 Operators
We have alrady seen basic arithmetic operations such as

+, -, *, /

Decimals are declared with a “.”, not a comma

1.8 not 1,8

Exponents are declared with ^, i.e. \(2^3\) is written as

2^3

For mathematical calculations, only parentheses () can be used.
Frequently used mathematical functions are

sqrt()            # square root
exp()             # exponential function
log()             # nat.  Logarithm
log(...,10)       # Logarithm with Base 10
abs()             # absolute value
round(...,x)      # rounding to x decimals.
pi 
exp(1)            # Eulers number
sin(),cos(),tan() # trigonemetric functions
min(), max()      # returns the lowest/highest value of a vector/matrix

Asa few examples enter the following calculations and make sure to understand the commands:

 1.8+2
 1.8-2
 1.8*2
 1.8/2
 2+2*3
 (2+2)*3
 2^3
 8^(1/3)
 3^2
 9^0.5
 2^2*2+2
 2^(2*((0.2+0.3)*(1+2)))+4
 sqrt(2)
 exp(1)
 exp(2)
 log(7.389056)
 log(exp(3))
 log(100,10)
 abs(1.8-2)
 round(sqrt(2),2)
 round(sqrt(2),4)
 pi
 sin(pi/2)
 sin(pi/2)
 sin(pi)
 tan(pi)
 x=2+3i
 y=4+1i
 x
 y
 x+y
 x*y

Attention:

 1.224606e-16

is interpreted as \(1.224606 \times 10^{-16}\). This is often exactly zero, but for internal memory purposes (R uses double-precision floating-point numbers and therefore only has up to 16 decimals), can be a rounding mistake.

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
1.5 Further Data Objects
Besides classical data objects such as scalars, vectors, and matrices there are three further data objects in R:
1.The array: A matrix but with more dimensions. Here is an example of a 2×2×2-dimensional array

myFirst.Array <- array(c(1:8), dim=c(2,2,2))


The list: In lists you can organize different kinds of data. E.g., consider the following example:


myFirst.List <- list("Some_Numbers" = c(66, 76, 55, 12, 4, 66, 8, 99), 
                     "Animals"      = c("Rabbit", "Cat", "Elefant"),
                     "My_Series"    = c(30:1)) 


The data frame: A data.frame is a list-object but with some more formal restrictions (e.g., equal number of rows for all columns). As indicated by its name, a data.frame-object is designed to store data:


myFirst.Dataframe <- data.frame("Credit_Default"   = c( 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1), 
                                "Age"              = c(35,41,55,36,44,26), 
                                "Loan_in_1000_EUR" = c(55,65,23,12,98,76))
crumbs: 1  The First Steps in R

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
1.6 R Help
There exist help files for all commands in R. For example consider the help file of the function sum(). You can access the help file with

?sum

The file usually contains the categories: Description, Usage, Arguments, Details, Value and References.
After the general description follows the syntax of the command. This usually indicates which (optional) arguments the command allows. Then follows na.rm, which indicates whether missing values (na) will be removed (rm). The default is FALSE.

 x<-c(1,2,NA,4,5)
 x

[1]  1  2 NA  4  5

sum(x)

[1] NA

sum(x,na.rm=T)

[1] 12


Details describes the exact calculation (trivial in this case), and some command specific characteristics. Value describes what is returned, in the case of sum() it is obviously a sum of numbers, given that numeric data was used as an input.

title: 1  The First Steps in R
text:
1.7 R Packages
There are tons of R packages that are useful for different aspects of data analysis. Some packages that can help you make beautiful plots and that you might want check out are the package ggplot2 and the collection of packages tidyverse. You can install the packages with install.packages(packagename). In order to use the package type library(package). The package has to be installed only once, but you have to load the package with library(package) every time you want to use it.

title: 2  Create and Load Data Sets
text:
2.1 Simulated Data
We start by considering data that is simulated by the user. We can create data sets by using functions like rnorm(), rexp() or runif(). After the data is created we can work with it as shown in the following example:
n = 100  # number of observations

Z = rnorm(n, mean = 5, sd = 3)      # draw from normal distribution 
mean(Z)

[1] 5.061976

sd(Z)

[1] 3.239456

E = rexp(n, rate = 3)           # draw data from exponential distribution 
mean(E)

[1] 0.3883579

sd(E)

[1] 0.4093271

U = runif(n, min = 3, max = 5)  # draw data from uniform distribution
mean(U)

[1] 4.072383

sd(U)

[1] 0.5690878
Analogous functions exist for many other distributions in R, and you can find them by searching on the web.
crumbs: 2  Create and Load Data Sets

title: 2  Create and Load Data Sets
text:
2.2 Load Datasets
It is also possible to work with observed data, which will be loaded into R. Here, we will use some real data, namely a movie database from IMDB that you can download here. The data set contains, among others, the budget, the revenue, and the average rating of movies.
Once the data is saved in your working directory, you can load it using

data_set = read.csv("tmdb_5000_movies.csv")

which stores the data in a data frame. You can use the View() function to look the data.
After the file is loaded, we can work with the data using $ to access certain parts of the data set such as

data_set$original_title[1:5]

[1] "Avatar"                                  
[2] "Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End"
[3] "Spectre"                                 
[4] "The Dark Knight Rises"                   
[5] "John Carter"                             

data_set$budget[1:5]

[1] 237000000 300000000 245000000 250000000 260000000

mean(data_set$budget[1:5])

[1] 258400000


We will return to this data set when we talk about regression analysis later.
Apart from read.csv there exist also read.dta, read.xls and many more to load suitable data sets.
Another important function is readRDS that is used to read in a data set that was saved using the function saveRDS. These functions can be useful in case properties of your R object are not preserved when saved in other formats, such as a csv file.
crumbs: 2  Create and Load Data Sets

title: 2  Create and Load Data Sets
text:
2.3 Save Datasets
There are also multiple ways to save your own data. While read.csv can be used to read in data from a csv file, its counterpart write.csv can be used to save a suitable object as a csv file. The most important arguments for this function are x, the object you want to save, and file, which provides the path where to save the file.
write.csv(data_set, <my_path>)
Similarly the function saveRDS allows you to save a generic R object to storage. One advantage of this function compared to write.csv is that it preserves properties of your object that might be lost when saved as a csv file. For example, conversions from factors to strings might occur when saving a data.frame as a csv file.
The package readxl and openxlsx from the tidyverse family can be used to read in and write to excel files, respectively. This format is usually not be the best option to store your data.

text:
2.4 Exercises II
Exercise 1:
Simulate a vector containing 10000 independent normally distributed random variables with means of 1 and variances of 2. How many of them are negative? What is the expected fraction of negative values?
Exercise 2:
Simulate u and v as independent log-normally distributed random vectors of size 200 each. Pick means and variances you like. Then let w be equal to u+v. Now calculate the following:

the sample means of u, v, and w

the sample variances of u, v, and w

all pairwise covariances

Exercise 3:
Take the objects you created in the previous exercises from this chapter and save them to storage in your preferred format. Then close your session, clean your workspace and read them in again. This might be tedious at first, but integrating the export of data into your workflow might save you from time costly mistakes in the future.

title: 3  Simple Programming
text:
3.1 The For-Loop
A for-loop is a procedure in which a particular routine is repeated and only an index variable is changed.
x=0
for (i in 1:3) { 
  x=x+i
  print(x)
}

[1] 1
[1] 3
[1] 6
We can also use it to study the behavior of the arithmetic mean
out = rep(0,100)
n = 20
for (i in 1:100) { 
  x = rnorm(n, mean = 0,sd = 1)
  out[i]=mean(x)
}
mean(out)

[1] -0.002921546

sd(out)

[1] 0.2265563

out = rep(0,100)
n = 200
for (i in 1:100) { 
  x = rnorm(n,mean = 0,sd = 1)
  out[i]=mean(x)
}
mean(out)

[1] 0.0007571941

sd(out)

[1] 0.06248292

title: 3  Simple Programming
text:
3.2 The If-Condition
Within a for-loop, it may be useful to perform arithmetic operations only under certain conditions. The basic syntax for this is

if (condition){
  statement  
  } 
else{
  alternative
  }

where else can remain unspecified.

###If-condition###
y <- c(1,4,5,2,7,8,2,4)
N <- length(y)
1:N
## 
y.sq <- numeric(N)#creates an empty numeric vector of length N

for(i in 1:N){ #initializing the for-loop
  y.sq[i] <- y[i]^2#every element of y.sq is replaced by the respective squared value.
  if(i == N){#only when this condition is met, i.e. in the last iteration of the loop 
    print(y.sq)#is the vector printed
  }
}

In shorter form the ifelse() command is an alternative.

ifelse(test, yes, no)

title: 4  Functions
text:
4.1 Function Definition
A function definition follows a specific structure.
my_function <- function(argument1, argument2){
  # here I describe what I want to do with my arguments
  # For example multiply them, assuming that they are numerical.
  
  my_return_value = argument1 * argument2
  
  # and using return() we tell our function what to return
  return(my_return_value)
} 

my_function(argument1 = 5, argument2 = 7)

[1] 35
The function can also be called without explicitly naming the arguments, but if you don’t know your code very well, this might lead to difficulties when somebody else or your future self might try to understand the code.
my_function(2,5)

[1] 10
Another useful feature is the definition of default values for your arguments such that they can be omitted when calling a function.
my_2nd_function <- function(argument1, argument2, greetings = FALSE){
  my_return_value <- argument1 * argument2
  if(greetings == TRUE){
    print("Hello user, the cake is a lie.")
  } 
  return(my_return_value)
} 

my_2nd_function(2, 7)

[1] 14

my_2nd_function(3, 12, TRUE)

[1] "Hello user, the cake is a lie."


[1] 36

title: 5  Plotting in R
text:
5.1 The Plot-Function
In its simplest form, the plot function in R delivers a scatterplot. In the call below, type = "p" could be omitted as it is the default value if the argument is not provided in the call.
x <- seq(0, 5, 0.1)
y <- rnorm(n = length(x))
plot(x = x, y = y, type = "p")
If we instead want a simple line plot or a combination of both, we can specify this behavior using the type argument.
z <- 2*x + rnorm(n = 51)
plot(x = x, y = z, type = "l")
plot(x = x, y = z, type = "b")
Other arguments to the plot function can be used to specify color, linetype (dashed etc.), linewidth, title, subtitle and many more. The help files ?plot and ?par can be very helpful when trying to achieve a specific look for your plot.
An example could look a little like this:
plot(x = x, y = y, type = "l", lty = 4, lwd = 2, col = "green", main = "Testplot")
If we want to show multiple things in one diagram it can be useful to plot multiple objects in one coordinate grid. R provides some ways to do so, the most simple ones being the lines function that works similar to the plot function and the abline function which can be used to add straight lines.
plot(x = x, y = y, type = "p", col = "green")
lines(x = x, y = z, type = "l", lwd = 2, lty = 4, col = "red")
abline(a=0, b=0.5, col = "blue")
As you may see from this plot, our y-axis is not adjusted to our newly added line. But we have a possibility to manually adjust the range of our axes if we choose to do so. This is done using the xlim and ylim arguments in the original plot function.
plot(x = x, y = y, type = "p", col = "green", xlim = c(0,5), ylim = c(-3, 12))
lines(x = x, y = z, type = "l", lwd = 2, lty = 4, col = "red")
abline(a=0, b=0.5, col = "blue")
It is also possible to plot functions like \(\sin(x)\) or the standard normal density.
plot(sin, xlim = c(-10, 10))






plot(dnorm, xlim = c(-4, 4))
There are many other useful plotting functions that are integrated in base R. We won’t cover all of them here, but instead focus on some of the most frequently needed.

title: 5  Plotting in R
text:
5.2 Histograms and Kernel Densities
Other useful plotting functions that are offered in the default R experience include histograms with the function hist. With a combination of plot and density we get access to kernel density plots. A kernel density estimator is a nonparametric estimator of density of random variable based on a sample. Details about the estimator are beyond the scope of these notes. In the settings where we will use them, the default choices of the estimator will yield accurate results. Combining our previous knowledge with these possibilities, we can create plots like the following (note: in hist the argument freq = FALSE leads to relative frequency instead of counts. See ?hist for more details.):

x <- rnorm(n = 20)
my_dens <- density(x)

hist(x, freq = FALSE, breaks = seq(-4, 4, 0.5), xlim = c(-4, 4)) 
lines(my_dens, col = "green", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(x = seq(-4, 4, 0.05), y = dnorm(seq(-4, 4, 0.05)), col = "red", lty = 1)







Further functions include barplots:

temperatures <- c(17,23,18,30,32,16,4,-3)
barplot(temperatures,
        ylim = c(-15, 35),
        main = "Daily Temperature",
        ylab = "Degree Celsius")







and piecharts:

slices <- c(8, 14, 9, 12, 4)
labels <- c("Apple", "Pumpkin", "Pork", "3.14", "American")
pie(slices, labels = labels, main = "Types of pie")







Another important part of plots - like comments in code - is a legible legend. R has built-in support for adding a legend to your plots. Going back to our combined plot from above, one can add a legend as shown in the following example. Here the x and y arguments specify the position of the legend in the plot and the other arguments specify its contents. Since a legend has to be customized for each plot, one should have a look in the documentation ?legend.

x <- seq(0, 5, 0.1)
y <- rnorm(n = length(x))
z <- 2*x + rnorm(n = 51)

plot(x = x, y = y, type = "p", col = "green", xlim = c(0,5), ylim = c(-3, 12))
lines(x = x, y = z, type = "l", lwd = 2, lty = 4, col = "red")
legend(x = 0, y = 10,
       legend = c("My green points", "My red line"),
       col = c("green", "red"),
       lty = c(1, 4),
       lwd = 2)







If one decides to pursue a tidyverse approach, the package ggplot allows for beautiful, heavily customized plots. An example can be seen below:

library(ggplot2)
library(ggforce)
library(hrbrthemes)

n = 800
x <- runif(n, min = -10, max = 10)
treatment <- ifelse(x>0,1,0)
y <- 0.2*x + treatment*3 + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.6)
visualise.data <- data.frame(x, treatment, y)

p1 <- ggplot(visualise.data, aes(x=x, y=y, colour = treatment == 1)) +
        labs(title = "Outcome Variable", y = "outcome variable", x = "assignment variable") +
        geom_point() + 
        geom_mark_ellipse(aes(filter = treatment == 1,
                              label = 'x \U02265 0')) + 
        geom_mark_ellipse(aes(filter = treatment == 0,
                              label = 'x < 0')) +
        geom_segment(aes(x = -10, y = -2, xend = 0, yend = 0), color = 'red', size = 1.5) +
        geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 3, xend = 10, yend = 5), color = 'red', size = 1.5) +
        #theme_ipsum(axis_title_size = 18) +
        theme(legend.position = "none",
              legend.title = element_text(size = 18)) +
        scale_colour_brewer(type = 'qual', palette = 'Dark2')

p1







The possibilities of ggplot2 are vast and can be intimidating, but it offers a consistent plotting experience integrated into a tidy data workflow using the tidyverse family of packages.

title: 6  Monte Carlo Simulations
text: 6.1 Some Important Concepts

title: 6  Monte Carlo Simulations
text:
6.1.1 Random Sample
Let \[
\{X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\}
\] denote an (i.i.d.) random sample, i.e., a collection of \(n\) random variables that all have the same distribution \(F_X\), \[
X_i\sim F_X\quad\text{for all}\quad i=1,\dots,n,
\] and that are independent of each other, \[
X_i \independent X_j \quad \text{for all} \quad i \neq j.
\]


The symbol \(\independent\) means independent of.
The abbreviation i.i.d. stands for independent and identically distributed.








Examples: \(F_X\) and Parameters of Interest \(\theta\)






Normal distribution: \(F_X = \mathcal{N}(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)\)


\(\theta = E(X) = \mu_X\), or
\(\theta = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \sigma^2_X\)



Chi-squared distribution: \(F_X = \chi^2_{\operatorname{df}}\)


\(\theta = E(X) = \operatorname{df}\), or
\(\theta = \operatorname{Var}(X) = 2\cdot \operatorname{df}\)



A distribution without a name: \(F_X\) is some unnamed distribution (most distributions have no name)


\(\theta = E(X)\), or

\(\theta = \operatorname{Median}(X)\), or
\(\theta = p\text{-Quantile}(X)\)



A multivariate distribution: \(F_{YX}\) is the joint distribution of \((Y, X^\top) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}\)


\(\theta = \beta\), the coefficient vector of the regression model \(Y_i = X_i^\top\beta + \varepsilon_i\)








6.1.2 Estimator
To estimate the unknown parameter \(\theta\), we use an estimator, which is simply a function of the random sample, \[
\hat{\theta}_n \equiv \hat{\theta}(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n).
\]
Since estimators are functions of random variables, they are random variables themselves.
🔊 Estimators are Random Variables❗
Thus, to understand an estimator, we need to know its statistical properties, i.e., its distribution or, at least, its mean and variance.
Observed data are just one observed realization of the random sample, \[
\{X_{1,\operatorname{obs}}, X_{2,\operatorname{obs}}, \ldots, X_{n,\operatorname{obs}}\}.
\] Each observed realization of the random sample yields a realization of the estimator, \[
\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}} \equiv \hat{\theta}(X_{1,\operatorname{obs}}, X_{2,\operatorname{obs}}, \ldots, X_{n,\operatorname{obs}}).
\]
This can be confusing: in practice, we typically have only one data set and, therefore, only one realization of the estimator. Still, we should keep in mind all the other data sets we could have obtained.

The following examples illustrate two random samples and their estimators:






Example: Estimating the Mean from an i.i.d. Random Sample





Let \[
\{X_1, \ldots, X_n\}
\] be an i.i.d. random sample with \(X_i \sim F_X\) for all \(i = 1, \dots, n\).






🤫 Psst … Secret Information



In this simulation, \(F_X = \mathcal{N}(\mu_X, \sigma^2_X)\) with \(\mu_X = 5\) and \(\sigma^2_X = 10\). In practice, \(F_X\), and thus \(\mu_X\) and \(\sigma^2_X\), are unknown.


We estimate the unknown mean \(\theta \equiv \mu_X\) by the sample mean \[
\hat\theta_n \equiv \hat\mu_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
\]
The following code generates one realization of the random sample. The fixed seed, set.seed(321), makes the pseudo-random numbers reproducible.

set.seed(321)

mean_X <- 5
var_X  <- 10
n      <- 10

sample_X <- rnorm(n = n, mean = mean_X, sd = sqrt(var_X))

The observed realization, stored in sample_X, \[
\{X_{1,\operatorname{obs}}, \ldots, X_{n,\operatorname{obs}}\} = \{10.39,\ 2.75,\ \dots,\ 3.25\}
\] yields the estimate \[
\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{i,\operatorname{obs}} = 5.47.
\]
A new sample yields a new estimate. The animation shows the observed sample (first frame, red) followed by further realizations of the random sample and of the estimator \(\hat\theta_n\) (blue).








Summary:


The data change from realization to realization, and so does the estimate. That is, \(\hat\theta_n\) is a random variable, and \(\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}}\) is just one of its realizations.
The realizations of \(\hat\theta_n\) lie close to the (usually unknown) true mean \(\mu_X = 5\). That is, the distribution of \(\hat\theta_n\) is concentrated around \(\mu_X\). This concentration increases with the sample size \(n\).











Example: Estimating Regression Coefficients from an i.i.d. Random Sample





Let \[
\{(Y_1, X_1^\top), \ldots, (Y_n, X_n^\top)\}
\] be an i.i.d. random sample with \((Y_i, X_i^\top) \sim F_{YX}\) for all \(i = 1, \dots, n\), where


\(Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + \varepsilon_i\) is the outcome, and
\(X_i \in \mathbb{R}^K\) is the vector of predictors of observation \(i\).








🤫 Psst … Secret Information



In this simulation, \(X_i = (1, X_{i2})^\top\) with \(X_{i2} \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 4]\), \(\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) independent of \(X_i\), and \(\beta = (2, -1)^\top\). Together, these choices fully specify the joint distribution \(F_{YX}\).
In practice, we assume (hopefully correctly) that we know the type of regression model, here the simple linear regression model \[
Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + \varepsilon_i \quad\text{with}\quad X_i = (1, X_{i2})^\top.
\]
However, we know only the model’s structure (here: an intercept and one predictor), not the entire model. In particular, we typically do not know:


the distribution of \(X_i\),
the distribution of \(\varepsilon_i\), and
the value of \(\beta\).


Thus, essential parts of \(F_{YX}\), such as \(\beta\), are unknown.


We estimate the unknown coefficient vector \(\theta \equiv \beta\) by the OLS estimator \[
\hat\theta_n \equiv \hat\beta_n = \left(X^\top X\right)^{-1} X^\top Y,
\] where \[
X = \begin{pmatrix}
X_1^\top \\ X_2^\top \\ \vdots \\ X_n^\top
\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
X_{11} & X_{12} & \cdots & X_{1K} \\
X_{21} & X_{22} & \cdots & X_{2K} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
X_{n1} & X_{n2} & \cdots & X_{nK}
\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
Y = \begin{pmatrix}
Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n
\end{pmatrix}
\] are the \(n \times K\) matrix of predictors and the \(n \times 1\) vector of outcomes.
The following code generates one realization of the random sample and computes the estimate.

set.seed(321)

n    <- 20
beta <- c(2, -1)

X   <- cbind(1, runif(n, min = 0, max = 4))   # first column: intercept
eps <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
Y   <- X %*% beta + eps

beta_hat <- solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% Y

The observed realization, stored in Y and X, \[
\{(Y_{1,\operatorname{obs}}, X_{1,\operatorname{obs}}^\top), \ldots, (Y_{n,\operatorname{obs}}, X_{n,\operatorname{obs}}^\top)\} = \{(-1.48,\ 1,\ 3.82),\ \dots,\ (-1.04,\ 1,\ 2.56)\}
\] yields the estimate, stored in beta_hat, \[
\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}} = (1.64,\ -0.79)^\top.
\]
A new sample yields a new estimate. The animation shows the observed sample (first frame, red) followed by further realizations of the random sample and of the estimator \(\hat\theta_n\) (blue).








Summary:


The data change from realization to realization, and so does the estimate. That is, \(\hat\theta_n\) is a random vector, and \(\hat{\theta}_{n,\operatorname{obs}}\) is just one of its realizations.
The estimated regression lines lie close to the (usually unknown) true line with \(\beta = (2, -1)^\top\). That is, the distribution of \(\hat\theta_n\) is concentrated around \(\beta\). This concentration increases with the sample size \(n\).








6.1.3 Bias, Variance, and Consistency of Estimators
Since an estimator is a random variable, it has a distribution and, typically, a mean and a variance. We use them to assess the quality of an estimator.







Definition 6.1 (Bias, Variance, Standard Error, and Mean Squared Error of \(\hat\theta_n\))  


The bias of \(\hat\theta_n\) is \[
\operatorname{Bias}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = E\left(\hat\theta_n\right) - \theta.
\]
The variance and the standard error of \(\hat\theta_n\) are \[
\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = E\left(\left(\hat\theta_n - E\left(\hat\theta_n\right)\right)^2\right)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{SE}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat\theta_n\right)}.
\]
The mean squared error of \(\hat\theta_n\) combines bias and variance, \[
\operatorname{MSE}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = E\left(\left(\hat\theta_n - \theta\right)^2\right) = \left(\operatorname{Bias}\left(\hat\theta_n\right)\right)^2 + \operatorname{Var}\left(\hat\theta_n\right).
\]






Bias. An estimator is called unbiased if \[
\operatorname{Bias}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = 0 \quad\text{for all}\quad n.
\] That is, averaged over all hypothetical data sets, the estimator equals \(\theta\). Unbiasedness holds for every fixed \(n\); it is a small-sample property. Many estimators, however, are biased for fixed \(n\). Then, we want them to be at least asymptotically unbiased, \[
\operatorname{Bias}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) \to 0 \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
\]
Variance. (Asymptotic) unbiasedness alone does not guarantee that the realizations of \(\hat\theta_n\) are close to \(\theta\): if \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n)\) is large, the realizations scatter widely around their mean, even in large samples. Therefore, we also want estimators to be consistent.







Definition 6.2 (Consistency of \(\hat\theta_n\)) An estimator \(\hat\theta_n\) is called (weakly) consistent if, for any (arbitrarily small) \(\varepsilon > 0\), \[
P\left(\left|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta\right| > \varepsilon\right) \rightarrow 0 \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
\] In short, we write \[
\hat{\theta}_n \rightarrow_P \theta \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
\]




That is, the realizations of a consistent estimator concentrate around \(\theta\) as the sample size grows.
A convenient way to check consistency is to verify that both the bias and the variance vanish, \[
\operatorname{Bias}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) \to 0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) \to 0
\quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty,
\] or, equivalently, that \(\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta_n) \to 0\). This condition is sufficient (but not necessary) for consistency; see the box below for a proof.






🤓 Nerd’s Box: A Sufficient Condition for Consistency





An estimator \(\hat\theta_n\) with \[
\operatorname{Bias}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) \to 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{Var}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) \to 0 \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty
\] is (weakly) consistent.
Proof. We use Chebyshev’s inequality: for any random variable \(Z\) with finite variance and any \(c > 0\), \[
P\left(\left|Z - E(Z)\right| > c\right) \leq \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{c^2}.
\]
Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Adding a zero, \(0 = -E(\hat\theta_n) + E(\hat\theta_n)\), and applying the triangle inequality, \(|a + b| \leq |a| + |b|\), yields \[
\left|\hat\theta_n - \theta\right|
\leq \left|\hat\theta_n - E\left(\hat\theta_n\right)\right| + \left|\operatorname{Bias}\left(\hat\theta_n\right)\right|.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta_n) \to 0\), there is an \(n_0\) such that \(|\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta_n)| \leq \varepsilon/2\) for all \(n \geq n_0\). Thus, for all \(n \geq n_0\), the event \(|\hat\theta_n - \theta| > \varepsilon\) implies \(|\hat\theta_n - E(\hat\theta_n)| > \varepsilon/2\), i.e., \[
\left\{\left|\hat\theta_n - \theta\right| > \varepsilon\right\} \subseteq \left\{\left|\hat\theta_n - E\left(\hat\theta_n\right)\right| > \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right\}.
\]
Applying Chebyshev’s inequality with \(Z = \hat\theta_n\) and \(c = \varepsilon/2\) yields \[
P\left(\left|\hat\theta_n - \theta\right| > \varepsilon\right)
\leq P\left(\left|\hat\theta_n - E\left(\hat\theta_n\right)\right| > \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)
\leq \frac{4 \operatorname{Var}\left(\hat\theta_n\right)}{\varepsilon^2}
\to 0 \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty. \quad \square
\]




6.1.4 Asymptotic Normality and Confidence Intervals
(Asymptotic) unbiasedness and consistency are minimum requirements for any estimator. For hypothesis tests and confidence intervals, however, we need more: the distribution of \(\hat\theta_n\).
Problem: The distribution of \(\hat\theta_n = \hat\theta(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) depends on the distribution \(F_X\) of the random sample, which is typically unknown.
Solution: Many estimators are asymptotically normal, which usually follows from a Central Limit Theorem (CLT): \[
\sqrt{n}\left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta\right) \rightarrow_D \mathcal{N}\left(0, \operatorname{AVar}\left(\hat{\theta}_n\right)\right) \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
\] Equivalently, for large \(n\), \[
\hat{\theta}_n \overset{a}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\left(\theta, \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{AVar}\left(\hat{\theta}_n\right)\right).
\] Here, the asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is (using \(\operatorname{Var}(aZ + b) = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(Z)\) for constants \(a, b\)) \[
\operatorname{AVar}\left(\hat{\theta}_n\right)
= \lim_{n\to\infty} \operatorname{Var}\left(\sqrt{n}\left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta\right)\right)
= \lim_{n\to\infty} n \operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{\theta}_n\right).
\]


Why scale by \(\sqrt{n}\)? For a consistent estimator, \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n) \to 0\). To obtain a non-degenerate limit distribution, we must scale appropriately. For most parametric estimators, the correct scaling factor is \(\sqrt{n}\).
Interpretation: The estimator, centered by \(\theta\) and scaled by \(\sqrt{n}\), is approximately normally distributed for large \(n\).


Such results hold only in the limit and are called large-sample properties. They allow us to test hypotheses and to construct confidence intervals. Let \(\widehat{\operatorname{AVar}}(\hat\theta_n)\) be a consistent estimator of \(\operatorname{AVar}(\hat\theta_n)\), and let \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\) be the significance level. Define the interval \[
\operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n = \left[\hat{\theta}_n - z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{AVar}}\left(\hat\theta_n\right)}{n}},\; \hat{\theta}_n + z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{AVar}}\left(\hat\theta_n\right)}{n}}\right],
\] where \[
z_{1-\alpha/2} = \Phi^{-1}\left(1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}\right)
\] denotes the \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of the standard normal distribution, and \(\Phi\) denotes the standard normal distribution function. Then \[
P\left(\theta \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\right) \rightarrow 1 - \alpha \quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty,
\] so \(\operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\) is an (asymptotic) \((1-\alpha)\cdot 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\theta\). For example, \(\alpha = 0.05\) yields \(z_{0.975} \approx 1.96\) and a \(95\%\) confidence interval.


Interpretation: Across all hypothetical data sets, \((1-\alpha)\cdot 100\%\) of the intervals contain \(\theta\). The interval changes from data set to data set; the parameter \(\theta\) does not.
Caveat: The \((1-\alpha)\cdot 100\%\) coverage holds only in the limit. For a fixed sample size \(n\), the actual coverage probability \(P(\theta \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n)\) can differ considerably from \(1-\alpha\): it can be smaller (under-coverage) or larger (over-coverage). In applications, the actual coverage probability is typically unknown.



6.1.5 Why Monte Carlo Simulations?
In practice, we always work with a fixed sample size \(n\). We therefore want to know the small-sample properties of \(\hat\theta_n\) for this \(n\), e.g.,


the bias \(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta_n)\),
the variance \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n)\) and the standard error \(\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta_n)\),
the mean squared error \(\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta_n)\), and
the actual coverage probability \(P(\theta \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n)\).


Problem: All of these depend on the distribution of \(\hat\theta_n\) for the given \(n\), which is typically unknown. There are three ways to derive or approximate it:



Exact derivation under a complete assumption on \(F_X\). For example, if \(X_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then \(\bar X_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\) for every \(n\).

Pro: exact for every \(n\).
Con: feasible only for simple estimators and distributions; the derivations are often cumbersome; wrong if the assumption on \(F_X\) is wrong.



Asymptotic approximation under weak assumptions on \(F_X\) (e.g., i.i.d. with finite variance), as in the previous section.

Pro: requires only weak assumptions on \(F_X\).
Con: exact only as \(n \to \infty\); can be poor for small \(n\).



Monte Carlo simulation under a complete assumption on \(F_X\).

Pro: approximates the exact distribution of \(\hat\theta_n\) with arbitrary precision for basically any \(F_X\), any estimator, and any \(n\); no derivations needed.
Con: the results hold only for the chosen \(F_X\).




In particular, Monte Carlo simulations let us check whether the asymptotic results of Option 2 are reliable for the sample sizes we face in practice.
How Do Monte Carlo Simulations Work?
Idea: Bias, variance, MSE, and coverage probability are all expectations, e.g., \[
\operatorname{MSE}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = E\left(\left(\hat\theta_n - \theta\right)^2\right)
\] and \[
P\left(\theta \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\right) = E\left(\mathbf{1}\left(\theta \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\right)\right),
\] where \(\mathbf{1}(\cdot)\) denotes the indicator function. By the law of large numbers, we can approximate expectations by sample means over many independent realizations, and a computer can generate as many realizations as we want.






Monte Carlo Simulation Algorithm



Choose a distribution \(F_X\), a sample size \(n\), and a large number of Monte Carlo replications \(B\) (e.g., \(B = 10{,}000\)). For each \(b = 1, \dots, B\):


Simulate data: Draw a realization of the random sample from \(F_X\) using a (pseudo-)random number generator, \[
\left\{X_{1,b}, \ldots, X_{n,b}\right\}.
\]
Compute the estimate: Compute the corresponding realization of the estimator (and, if needed, of the confidence interval \(\operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_{n,b}\) or a test statistic), \[
\hat\theta_{n,b} = \hat\theta\left(X_{1,b}, \ldots, X_{n,b}\right).
\]


This yields \(B\) independent realizations \(\hat\theta_{n,1}, \ldots, \hat\theta_{n,B}\) of the estimator.


From these \(B\) realizations, we compute the Monte Carlo approximations:


Bias: \[
\widehat{\operatorname{Bias}}_{\operatorname{MC}}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = \bar\theta_{n,B} - \theta,
\quad\text{where}\quad
\bar\theta_{n,B} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat\theta_{n,b}.
\]
Variance: \[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\operatorname{MC}}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \left(\hat\theta_{n,b} - \bar\theta_{n,B}\right)^2.
\]
Mean squared error: \[
\widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}_{\operatorname{MC}}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \left(\hat\theta_{n,b} - \theta\right)^2.
\]
Coverage probability (the share of simulated intervals that contain \(\theta\)): \[
\widehat{P}_{\operatorname{MC}}\left(\theta \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\right) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\left(\theta \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_{n,b}\right).
\]


By the law of large numbers, these approximations become arbitrarily precise as \(B \to \infty\), e.g., \[
\widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}_{\operatorname{MC}}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) \rightarrow_P \operatorname{MSE}\left(\hat\theta_n\right) \quad\text{as}\quad B \to \infty.
\] Likewise, the empirical distribution function of \(\hat\theta_{n,1}, \ldots, \hat\theta_{n,B}\) approximates the entire distribution function of \(\hat\theta_n\) as \(B \to \infty\) (Glivenko–Cantelli theorem).






Two Different “Sample Sizes”





\(n\) is the sample size of one data set. It is part of the setup we investigate: \(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta_n)\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n)\), etc. depend on it.
\(B\) is the number of simulated data sets. It controls only the precision of the Monte Carlo approximations and should be as large as computationally feasible.




⚠️ Monte Carlo results hold only for the chosen \(F_X\) and \(n\). Therefore, we typically repeat the simulation for several distributions \(F_X\) (e.g., normal, skewed, heavy-tailed) and several sample sizes \(n\) (small, intermediate, and large).

title: 6  Monte Carlo Simulations
text:
6.2 Simulation Example: The Sample Mean
This example walks through a complete Monte Carlo simulation in five steps. Use it as a blueprint for your own simulations.

6.2.1 Step 1: Define the Estimator and the Questions
Let \[
\{X_1, \ldots, X_n\}
\] be an i.i.d. random sample with \[
X_i \sim F_X,
\] and let

\(\mu = E(X)\)
\(\sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X).\)

The parameter of interest is thus the mean, \(\theta = \mu\). We estimate it by the sample mean \[
\hat\mu_n = \bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
\] and construct the asymptotic confidence interval from above: \[
\operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n = \left[\bar X_n - z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{s_n}{\sqrt{n}},\; \bar X_n + z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{s_n}{\sqrt{n}}\right],
\] where \[
s_n = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X_n)^2}
\] is the sample standard deviation, a consistent estimator of \(\sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{AVar}(\bar X_n)}\).






🤓 Nerd’s Box: The Asymptotic Variance of \(\bar X_n\)





Since \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) are independent, the variance of their sum is the sum of their variances. Since they are identically distributed, \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2\) for all \(i\). Using \(\operatorname{Var}(aZ) = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(Z)\), we get \[\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}\left(\bar X_n\right)
&= \operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)
= \frac{1}{n^2}\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)\\[2ex]
&= \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}\left(X_i\right)
= \frac{1}{n^2}\, n\, \sigma^2
= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\end{align*}\] Thus, by the definition of the asymptotic variance, \[
\operatorname{AVar}\left(\bar X_n\right)
= \lim_{n\to\infty} n \operatorname{Var}\left(\bar X_n\right)
= \lim_{n\to\infty} n \, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}
= \sigma^2.
\] Hence, \(\sqrt{\operatorname{AVar}(\bar X_n)/n} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}\), which \(\operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\) estimates by \(s_n/\sqrt{n}\).



What Does Theory Already Tell Us?
For any \(F_X\) with finite variance and any \(n\), \[
\operatorname{Bias}\left(\bar X_n\right) = 0
\] and \[
\operatorname{Var}\left(\bar X_n\right) = \operatorname{MSE}\left(\bar X_n\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\] The coverage probability, however, is known only in the limit: \[
P(\mu \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n) \to 1 - \alpha\quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
\]






🤓 Nerd’s Box: Derivations of Bias, Variance, MSE, and Coverage





Bias. By the linearity of the expectation and \(E(X_i) = \mu\) for all \(i\), \[
E\left(\bar X_n\right) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E\left(X_i\right) = \frac{1}{n}\, n\, \mu = \mu
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\operatorname{Bias}\left(\bar X_n\right) = E\left(\bar X_n\right) - \mu = 0.
\]
Variance. As shown in the previous box (using independence), \[
\operatorname{Var}\left(\bar X_n\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]
MSE. By the bias–variance decomposition, \[
\operatorname{MSE}\left(\bar X_n\right) = \left(\operatorname{Bias}\left(\bar X_n\right)\right)^2 + \operatorname{Var}\left(\bar X_n\right) = 0 + \frac{\sigma^2}{n} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]
Coverage probability. The interval contains \(\mu\) if and only if the \(t\)-statistic is small: \[
\mu \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
\left|T_n\right| \leq z_{1-\alpha/2},
\quad\text{where}\quad
T_n = \frac{\sqrt{n}\left(\bar X_n - \mu\right)}{s_n}.
\] Thus, \(P(\mu \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n) = P(|T_n| \leq z_{1-\alpha/2})\). As \(n \to \infty\),


\(\sqrt{n}(\bar X_n - \mu)/\sigma \rightarrow_D \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) by the CLT, and
\(s_n \rightarrow_P \sigma\) by the law of large numbers.


Together (Slutsky’s theorem), \(T_n \rightarrow_D \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). Therefore, as \(n\to\infty,\) \[
P\left(\left|T_n\right| \leq z_{1-\alpha/2}\right)
\to \Phi\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) - \Phi\left(-z_{1-\alpha/2}\right)
= \left(1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}\right) - \frac{\alpha}{2}
= 1 - \alpha.
\]
Why only in the limit? For fixed \(n\), the distribution of \(T_n\) depends on the shape of \(F_X\) and is typically unknown.
One exception is normal data: if \(F_X = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then \(T_n\) follows a \(t\)-distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom. Hence, the exact coverage is \[
P\left(\mu \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\right) = 2\, F_{t_{n-1}}\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) - 1 < 1 - \alpha,
\] where \(F_{t_{n-1}}\) denotes the distribution function of the \(t_{n-1}\)-distribution. For \(\alpha = 0.05\), this gives \(0.878\) for \(n = 5\), \(0.935\) for \(n = 20\), and \(0.947\) for \(n = 100\). These values serve as a benchmark for the simulation results below. For skewed data such as \(\chi^2_1\), no such formula is available, so we need a simulation.



Questions for the Simulation


Do the Monte Carlo approximations of bias, variance, and MSE match the theory? (This is mainly a sanity check of our code.)
How close is the actual coverage probability to \(1 - \alpha\) for small \(n\), and does it depend on the shape of \(F_X\)? (This is the open question.)



6.2.2 Step 2: Choose the Simulation Design
We compare two distributions with the same mean and variance but different shapes:


Symmetric: \(F_X = \mathcal{N}(1, 2)\).
Right-skewed: \(F_X = \chi^2_1\), which also has \(E(X) = 1\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = 2\).


Thus, \(\mu = 1\) and \(\sigma^2 = 2\) in both cases. Any difference between the two cases is due to the shape of \(F_X\) alone. The remaining design parameters are:


sample sizes \(n \in \{5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500\}\),
significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\), i.e., a nominal coverage of \(95\%\),
\(B = 10{,}000\) Monte Carlo replications per design, and
a fixed seed for reproducibility.









Figure 6.1: The two data distributions \(F_X\). Both have mean \(\mu = 1\) (dashed line) and variance \(\sigma^2 = 2\).





6.2.3 Step 3: Write the Simulation Code
We implement the algorithm from above in three parts.
(a) Set the design parameters.

set.seed(123)

mu    <- 1                             # true mean E(X)
sigma <- sqrt(2)                       # true standard deviation sd(X)
n_seq <- c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500)    # sample sizes
B     <- 10000                         # Monte Carlo replications
alpha <- 0.05                          # significance level
z     <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)          # standard normal quantile

## Random number generators for the two distributions F_X
r_FX <- list(
  "Normal"     = function(n) rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma),
  "Chi-square" = function(n) rchisq(n, df = 1)
)

(b) Write a function for one replication. It performs Steps 1 and 2 of the algorithm: it simulates one data set and returns the estimate and whether the confidence interval contains \(\mu\).

one_replication <- function(n, r_X) {
  X_sim    <- r_X(n)                               # 1. simulate data
  mu_hat   <- mean(X_sim)                          # 2. compute estimate
  se_hat   <- sd(X_sim) / sqrt(n)                  #    and the CI
  CI_lower <- mu_hat - z * se_hat
  CI_upper <- mu_hat + z * se_hat
  covers   <- (CI_lower <= mu) & (mu <= CI_upper)
  c(mu_hat = mu_hat, covers = covers)
}

(c) Repeat \(B\) times for each design and compute the Monte Carlo approximations.

results   <- data.frame()
estimates <- list()                                # keep realizations for plots

for (dist in names(r_FX)) {
  for (n in n_seq) {
    sim <- replicate(B, one_replication(n = n, r_X = r_FX[[dist]]))
    mu_hat_B <- sim["mu_hat", ]                    # B realizations of the estimator
    covers_B <- sim["covers", ]                    # B coverage indicators (0/1)

    estimates[[paste(dist, n)]] <- mu_hat_B
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      dist     = dist,
      n        = n,
      Bias     = mean(mu_hat_B) - mu,
      Var      = mean((mu_hat_B - mean(mu_hat_B))^2),
      Var_theo = sigma^2 / n,
      MSE      = mean((mu_hat_B - mu)^2),
      Coverage = mean(covers_B)
    ))
  }
}

6.2.5 Step 5: Interpret the Results
Question 1: Bias, variance, and MSE. The simulation confirms the theory (Table 6.1 and Figure 6.3, left):


The bias is close to zero for all designs. The remaining deviations are of the order of the Monte Carlo standard error of the bias, \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)/B}\), e.g., \(\sqrt{0.4/10{,}000} \approx 0.006\) for \(n = 5\).
The variance and the MSE match \(\sigma^2/n\) and decrease at rate \(1/n\), i.e., with slope \(-1\) on log-log scales.
Both distributions yield the same results, since these properties depend on \(F_X\) only through \(\sigma^2\).


Question 2: Coverage. Here the simulation reveals what asymptotic theory cannot (Table 6.1 and Figure 6.3, right):


Under-coverage for small \(n\): For \(n = 5\), the coverage is only 0.880 (normal) and 0.759 (\(\chi^2_1\)) instead of \(0.95\). Even for normal data, the interval is too short because it ignores the estimation uncertainty in \(s_n\). (Using the \(t_{n-1}\)-quantile instead of \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) would fix this for normal data, but not for skewed data.)
The shape of \(F_X\) matters: Under the skewed \(\chi^2_1\) distribution, the convergence to \(0.95\) is much slower. Even for \(n = 100\), the coverage is 0.931. The reason is visible in Figure 6.2: for small \(n\), the distribution of \(\bar X_n\) is still skewed, so the normal approximation behind the interval is poor.
Large \(n\): For \(n = 500\), the coverage is close to \(0.95\) in both cases, as the CLT predicts.








How Precise Are the Monte Carlo Results?



Monte Carlo approximations are themselves estimates based on \(B\) replications. For a coverage probability \(p\), the Monte Carlo standard error is \[
\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{B}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{0.95 \cdot 0.05}{10{,}000}} \approx 0.002.
\] Thus, deviations from \(0.95\) within about \(\pm 0.004\) (the gray band in Figure 6.3) can be pure Monte Carlo error, while the under-coverage found above is real. To halve the Monte Carlo error, quadruple \(B\).




6.2.6 Blueprint: Designing Your Own Simulation


Define the estimator and the questions. Which estimator (or test, or interval)? Which properties (bias, variance, MSE, coverage, rejection rates)? What does theory already tell you?
Choose the design. Which distributions \(F_X\) (include cases where the assumptions are stressed, e.g., skewness or heavy tails)? Which sample sizes \(n\)? Which number of replications \(B\)? Fix a seed for the (pseudo) random number generator(s).
Write the code. Write a function for one replication (simulate data, compute estimate), repeat it \(B\) times for each design, and store the results in a data frame.
Present the results. Use tables for exact numbers and figures for patterns across \(n\) and \(F_X\). Always show the target value (e.g., \(\mu\), \(\sigma^2/n\), or \(1-\alpha\)) for comparison.
Interpret the results. Answer each question from Step 1, and account for Monte Carlo error before drawing conclusions.

title: 6  Monte Carlo Simulations
text:
6.3 Simulation Example: Hypothesis Testing
We now apply the blueprint to a hypothesis test about \(\mu\), using the same design as above: \(F_X \in \{\mathcal{N}(1, 2), \chi^2_1\}\), \(\sigma^2 = 2\), and \(B = 10{,}000\).


6.3.1 Step 1: Define the Test and the Questions
Consider the test of \[
H_0\colon \mu = \mu_0 \quad\text{against}\quad H_1\colon \mu \neq \mu_0
\] based on the \(t\)-statistic \[
T_n = \frac{\sqrt{n}\left(\bar X_n - \mu_0\right)}{s_n}.
\] We reject \(H_0\) if \(|T_n| > z_{1-\alpha/2}\). By the CLT, as \(n \to \infty\),


the size, i.e., the rejection probability if \(H_0\) is true, converges to \(\alpha\), and
the power, i.e., the rejection probability if \(H_0\) is false, converges to \(1\).


How large are size and power for small \(n\)?






Tests and Confidence Intervals



We reject \(H_0\colon \mu = \mu_0\) if and only if \(\mu_0 \notin \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\). Thus, under \(H_0\), \[
P\left(\text{reject } H_0\right) = 1 - P\left(\mu_0 \in \operatorname{CI}^{1-\alpha}_n\right),
\] i.e., the size is one minus the coverage probability. The under-coverage found above therefore implies that the test rejects a true \(H_0\) too often.



6.3.2 Step 2: Choose the Simulation Design
We test \(\mu_0 = 1\) and vary the true mean \(\mu\) over a grid from \(0\) to \(2\). To shift the mean without changing the shape of \(F_X\), we generate \[
X_i = \mu + U_i,
\] where \(U_i\) has mean zero and variance \(2\): either \(U_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2)\) or \(U_i \sim \chi^2_1 - 1\). We consider \(n \in \{20, 100\}\).

6.3.3 Step 3: Write the Simulation Code
As before, we write a function for one replication and repeat it \(B\) times for each design.

mu_0    <- 1                                    # hypothesized mean
mu_grid <- seq(0, 2, by = 0.1)                  # true means
n_test  <- c(20, 100)                           # sample sizes

## Random number generators for the mean-zero errors U
r_U <- list(
  "Normal"     = function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma),
  "Chi-square" = function(n) rchisq(n, df = 1) - 1
)

one_test <- function(n, mu_true, r_U_dist) {
  X_sim  <- mu_true + r_U_dist(n)                         # 1. simulate data
  T_stat <- sqrt(n) * (mean(X_sim) - mu_0) / sd(X_sim)   # 2. test statistic
  abs(T_stat) > z                                         #    reject H0?
}

test_results <- data.frame()
for (dist in names(r_U)) {
  for (n in n_test) {
    for (mu_true in mu_grid) {
      reject_B <- replicate(B, one_test(n = n, mu_true = mu_true,
                                        r_U_dist = r_U[[dist]]))
      test_results <- rbind(test_results, data.frame(
        dist = dist, n = n, mu = mu_true,
        Reject = mean(reject_B)                 # MC rejection probability
      ))
    }
  }
}


6.3.4 Steps 4 and 5: Present and Interpret the Results
Figure 6.4 shows the rejection probabilities as functions of the true mean \(\mu\).







Figure 6.4: Monte Carlo rejection probabilities of the \(t\)-test of \(H_0\colon \mu = 1\) as functions of the true mean \(\mu\). At \(\mu = 1\) (dotted line), the curves show the size; elsewhere, they show the power. The dashed line marks \(\alpha = 0.05\).






Size: At \(\mu = \mu_0\), the rejection probability for \(n = 20\) is 0.061 (normal) and 0.119 (\(\chi^2_1\)) instead of \(\alpha = 0.05\). As expected, this is approximately one minus the coverage probabilities in Table 6.1; the small differences are Monte Carlo error.
Power: The further \(\mu\) is from \(\mu_0\), the higher the power. For \(n = 100\), the power is close to \(1\) already for \(|\mu - \mu_0| \geq 0.6\); for \(n = 20\), a much larger distance is needed.
Skewness: Under \(\chi^2_1\), the power curve is asymmetric. For \(n = 20\) and \(\mu = 1.3\), the power (0.096) is even smaller than the size. Again, the normal approximation is poor for skewed data and small \(n\).

6.4 Exercises VI
Use the blueprint above for both exercises.
Exercise 1:
Suppose \(X \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 2]\), where \(\mathcal{U}[0, 2]\) denotes the uniform distribution on the interval \([0, 2]\). It is easy to show (make sure to verify this!) that \(E(X) = 1\). Now repeat the following two steps at least \(1{,}000\) times:

Draw a random sample of size \(n = 20\) from the distribution of \(X\).
Compute the sample mean and a \(95\%\) confidence interval for \(E(X)\) from this sample.

You now have \(1{,}000\) sample means and \(1{,}000\) confidence intervals. Use them to answer the following questions:

What is the average of your \(1{,}000\) sample means?
What is the standard deviation of your \(1{,}000\) sample means?
How often does the \(95\%\) confidence interval contain \(E(X)\)?

Exercise 2:
In this exercise, we use the Monte Carlo method to approximate the number \(\pi\). Randomly draw \(n\) points from a square and count how many of them lie inside the square’s incircle. Based on this count and the formula for the area of a circle, compute an approximation of \(\pi\).

title: 7  Regression Analysis
text:
7.1 Basic Linear Model
You have probably all learnt about the linear regression model in a previous econometrics class where \[Y =  \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \ldots + \beta_{k} X_{k} + \beta_{k+1} + e \] and \[E(e \mid X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{k}) = 0.\] That is, the conditional mean of the outcome variable \(Y\) is a linear function of the regressors \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{k}\).
When we have a random sample of size \(n\), we can also write \[Y_i = \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_k X_{ik} + \beta_{k+1} +  e_i, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.\] Our goal is to estimate the coefficients \(\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_{k+1}\) using the data \(\{Y_i, X_{i1},X_{i2},\ldots, X_{ik}\}^n_{i=1}\).

title: 7  Regression Analysis
text:
7.3 Exercises VII
Exercise 1:
In the previous section, we looked at Monte Carlo simulations in a very simple setting. We can analyze analogous issues in other settings, such as the linear regression model. Also in this case, we have parameters (the regression coefficients) and estimators (the OLS estimators). The parameters are random and have certain known small and large sample properties that you discussed in the theoretical part of the class. Many other small sample properties, such as actual coverage rates of confidence intervals are unknown, but can be studies in Monte Carlo simulations.
Let \[Y_i = \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2}+  \beta_3 + e_i, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.\] where \[\begin{pmatrix}X_{i1}\\X_{i2}\\\end{pmatrix} \sim N\left( \begin{pmatrix}2\\-3 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}1& \rho  \\ \rho &1 \end{pmatrix} \right)\] and \((\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3) = (2,1,-1)\). Let \(e_i \sim U[-2,2]\) and assume that \(e_i\) is independent of \((X_{i1},X_{i2})\). Assume that the data is a random sample. Let \((\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\beta}_2, \hat{\beta}_3 )\) be the OLS estimator of \((\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3)\).
For different values of \(n\) and \(\rho\) use simulations to calculate


\(E(\hat{\beta}_1)\),

\(Var(\hat{\beta}_1)\),
the probability that \(\beta_1\) is in a \(95\%\) confidence interval,
the expected length of the confidence interval,
the probability that we reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 2\) using a two-sided t-test and a \(1\%\) significance level, and
the probability that we reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 1.8\) using a two-sided t-test and a \(1\%\) significance level.

Discuss the results.
How do you think the results will change if \(X_{i1}\) and \(e_i\) are correlated?
Exercise 2:
Start with the help file ?lm() of the linear model - one of the functions most often used in R - and try to answer these questions:

How do you estimate a model without a constant?
In what setting could na.action = na.exclude be more useful to you than the function’s default value?
For a given lm-object, what does the function summary do?

Exercise 3:
Assume that \(X \sim U[0,1]\) and \(Y \sim U[0,1]\) are independent random variables. For different sample sizes (\(n \in\{ 2, 5, 10, 100, 1000\}\)) draw two i.i.d. samples of \(X\) and \(Y\) and regress \(Y\) on \(X\) for both samples. Using a Monte-Carlo simulation, approximate the probability that the two corresponding regression lines intersect on \([0,1]\times  [0,1]\). Do the results depend on the sample size?

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
9.1 Positron for the First Time
Positron is not only an IDE for R, but also for Python. For installation just follow the instructions on https://positron.posit.co/download.html
In addition, you need a Python installation. Positron detects installed Python versions automatically and lets you pick one as interpreter (the button in the upper right corner of the window). A good practice is to create a virtual environment for each project, i.e., a folder (usually called .venv) that contains the Python interpreter together with all packages you install for this project. In Positron you can create one via the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) and the command Python: Create Environment.
When you open Positron, its window is typically split into the following areas:
Some other terms that will be useful:
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
The editor showing your script file, which is an ordinary text file with suffix .py. For instance, yourFavoritFileName.py. This file contains your code.
The Session pane showing all objects (variables) we have defined in the environment.
The Plots and Help panes showing plots and help files.
The Console, which allows you to type commands and display results.
The Explorer (left) showing the files in your current project folder.



Working directory: The file-directory you are working in. Useful commands: with os.getcwd() you get the location of your current working directory and os.chdir() allows you to set a new location for it (both functions are part of the module os, which you load with import os). This is very useful when you would like to load or save several files. You can just set your working directory globally and all files can be loaded or will be saved into this directory.
Workspace (namespace): This is where all objects you use (e.g., data, matrices, vectors, variables, functions, etc.) are stored during your session. Useful commands in the Positron console: %who shows all variables in our current workspace and %reset -f deletes all elements in our current workspace. It is also possible to remove only some objects with del object1, object2.
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
9.2 Simple Calculations
We start with a very basic calculation. Let’s type 1+1 into the console window and press enter. We get

1+1 # first calculation

2


i.e. the result of the calculation is returned.
Note that everything that is written after the #-sign is ignored by Python, which is very useful to comment your code. The second window above shows the output.
Let’s consider a second calculation

1+2+3+ # second calculation


  Cell In[2], line 1
    1+2+3+ # second calculation
           ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax




This calculation ended with an error. The reason is that the command can only processed if entered correctly.

1+2+3+4 # second calculation

10


A similar thing happens when parentheses are not closed.

2*(2+3


  Cell In[4], line 1
    2*(2+3
          ^
_IncompleteInputError: incomplete input




It will be helpful to use a script file, such as yourFavoritFileName.py, to store your Python commands. Otherwise, you would have to type your code again when an error occurred. You can send single lines or marked regions of your Python code to the console by pressing the keys STRG+ENTER.
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
9.3 Assigments and Matrix Algebra
The assignment operator will be your most often used tool. Here is an example where a scalar variable is created:

x = 9
x

9



x+1

10


Note: If you run several lines at once (e.g., a code block), Python only shows the result of the last line. If you want to see several results, use the print() function:

x = 9
print(x)
print(x+1)

9
10


In Python, assignments are always done with the = operator (there is no <- as in R). More on Python style recommendations can be found in the PEP 8 style guide.
We consider now a vector, an object you will use frequently. Python itself does not have vectors and matrices in the mathematical sense. They are provided by the package NumPy, which we load (under the usual short name np) with

import numpy as np

A vector is then created with np.array():

z = np.array([1,3,5,6])
z

array([1, 3, 5, 6])


As discussed, %who states the content of the workspace, whereas %reset -f deletes the workspace.

%who

np   x   z   



%reset -f
%who

Interactive namespace is empty.


Note that %reset -f also removed the NumPy package from the workspace, so we have to load it again.

import numpy as np

In the next step we will consider some vector multiplication. There are three different ways to multiply a vector, namely element by element, using the inner product, or using the outer product. Element by element gives you a vector of the same dimension.

z = np.array([1,3,5,6])
z*z                #multiplication element by element

array([ 1,  9, 25, 36])


The attribute .T gives the transpose of a vector (or matrix). It is therefore tempting to calculate the inner product as

z.T*z                #multiplication inner product?

array([ 1,  9, 25, 36])


but this does not give the desired answer. (A one-dimensional NumPy array is neither a row nor a column vector, so transposing it does not change anything.) Instead, you have to use the matrix multiplication operator @

z = np.array([1,3,5,6])
z @ z                #multiplication inner product

np.int64(71)


The output np.int64(71) simply means: the number 71, stored as a NumPy integer. (With print(z @ z) you would only see 71.) Note that, in contrast to R, NumPy stores zTz as a number and not as a matrix.

type(z @ z)

numpy.int64



type(z)

numpy.ndarray


Finally, we have the outer product that gives us a matrix

z = np.array([1,3,5,6])
np.outer(z, z)                #multiplication outer product

array([[ 1,  3,  5,  6],
       [ 3,  9, 15, 18],
       [ 5, 15, 25, 30],
       [ 6, 18, 30, 36]])


In general, be very careful with @ versus *. They are often both feasible, but yield different results!
You can also multiply a vector with a scalar:

z*4

array([ 4, 12, 20, 24])


A strength of NumPy is that operations can be conducted for each element of the vector in one statement

print(z**2)
print(np.log(z))
print((z-np.mean(z))/np.std(z, ddof=1))

[ 1  9 25 36]
[0.         1.09861229 1.60943791 1.79175947]
[-1.24021595 -0.33824071  0.56373452  1.01472214]


Note: np.std() divides by \(n\) by default. With the argument ddof=1 it divides by \(n-1\), as R’s sd() does.
So far, we have seen the function np.array() that can be used to combine objects. All function calls use the same general notation: a function name is always followed by round parentheses. Sometimes, the parentheses include arguments, such as

z = np.arange(start = 1, stop = 6, step = 1)
z

array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])


Note that the stop value is not included.
With square brackets you can access particular elements, such as

z[0:3]                  #refer to particular elements

array([1, 2, 3])


Attention: In Python, counting starts at 0, i.e., z[0] is the first element of z. Moreover, z[0:3] includes the elements at positions 0, 1, and 2, but not the element at position 3.
We will next define a matrix and perform matrix-vector multiplication.

M = np.arange(1, 10).reshape((3,3), order = "F")    # define matrix M (filled column by column, as in R)
print(M)
print(M.shape)                                     # dimension of M
print(z.shape)                                     # dimension of z: (5,) means one-dimensional with 5 elements
print(len(z))                                      # number of elements of z

[[1 4 7]
 [2 5 8]
 [3 6 9]]
(3, 3)
(5,)
5


Element-by-element multiplication for M is given by

M * M

array([[ 1, 16, 49],
       [ 4, 25, 64],
       [ 9, 36, 81]])


Standard matrix multiplication is again done using @ such as

M @ M

array([[ 30,  66, 102],
       [ 36,  81, 126],
       [ 42,  96, 150]])



M.T @ M

array([[ 14,  32,  50],
       [ 32,  77, 122],
       [ 50, 122, 194]])


If matrices and vectors have suitable dimensions, you can multiply them as follows:

M @ z[0:3]

array([30, 36, 42])


Similar to before, with square brackets you can access particular elements, such as

print(M[:,2])                 # state the third column of M
print(M[2,2])                 # state element in the third column and third row of M

[7 8 9]
9


Here are some more examples:

M[:,0]                 # first column of M
M[2,2]                 # element in the third column and third row of M
z[[0,3]]               # first and fourth element of z

Logical statements are also very useful. For example, if you want to know which elements in the first column of matrix M are strictly greater than 2:

# See which elements:
print(M[:,0]>2)
# and extract the elements
print(M[M[:,0]>2,0])

[False False  True]
[3]


Note: Logical operations return so-called boolean objects, i.e., either a True or a False. For instance, if we ask Python whether 1>2 we get the answer False.
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
9.4 Operators
We have already seen basic arithmetic operations such as

+, -, *, /

Decimals are declared with a “.”, not a comma

1.8 not 1,8

Exponents are declared with **, i.e. \(2^3\) is written as

2**3

Attention: In contrast to R, 2^3 does not compute \(2^3\) in Python (^ is the “bitwise exclusive or” operator).
For mathematical calculations, only parentheses () can be used.
Frequently used mathematical functions are (most of them are provided by NumPy)

np.sqrt()                # square root
np.exp()                 # exponential function
np.log()                 # nat.  Logarithm
np.log10()               # Logarithm with Base 10
abs()                    # absolute value
round(...,x)             # rounding to x decimals.
np.pi
np.e                     # Eulers number
np.sin(),np.cos(),np.tan() # trigonemetric functions
np.min(), np.max()       # returns the lowest/highest value of a vector/matrix

As a few examples enter the following calculations and make sure to understand the commands:

1.8+2
1.8-2
1.8*2
1.8/2
2+2*3
(2+2)*3
2**3
8**(1/3)
3**2
9**0.5
2**2*2+2
2**(2*((0.2+0.3)*(1+2)))+4
np.sqrt(2)
np.exp(1)
np.exp(2)
np.log(7.389056)
np.log(np.exp(3))
np.log10(100)
abs(1.8-2)
round(np.sqrt(2),2)
round(np.sqrt(2),4)
np.pi
np.sin(np.pi/2)
np.sin(np.pi)
np.tan(np.pi)
x=2+3j     # complex numbers: Python uses j instead of i
y=4+1j
x
y
x+y
x*y

Attention:

1.2246467991473532e-16

is interpreted as \(1.2246467991473532 \times 10^{-16}\). This is often exactly zero, but for internal memory purposes (Python uses double-precision floating-point numbers and therefore only has up to 16 decimals), can be a rounding mistake.
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
9.5 Further Data Objects
Besides classical data objects such as scalars, vectors, and matrices there are three further data objects that we will use frequently:

The array: A NumPy array can have more than two dimensions. Here is an example of a 2×2×2-dimensional array


myFirst_Array = np.arange(1, 9).reshape((2,2,2), order = "F")


The dictionary: In dicts you can organize different kinds of data (this is the counterpart of R’s list). E.g., consider the following example:


myFirst_Dict = {"Some_Numbers": [66, 76, 55, 12, 4, 66, 8, 99],
                "Animals"     : ["Rabbit", "Cat", "Elefant"],
                "My_Series"   : list(range(30, 0, -1))}

Python also has a data object called list, e.g., ["Rabbit", "Cat", "Elefant"], which is simply an ordered collection of arbitrary objects.

The data frame: Data frames are provided by the package pandas. A DataFrame is designed to store data, where each column can have a different type, but all columns have the same number of rows:


import pandas as pd

myFirst_Dataframe = pd.DataFrame({"Credit_Default"  : [ 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1],
                                  "Age"             : [35,41,55,36,44,26],
                                  "Loan_in_1000_EUR": [55,65,23,12,98,76]})
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
9.6 Python Help
There exist help files for all commands in Python. For example consider the help file of the function np.sum(). You can access the help file with

help(np.sum)

or, in the Positron console, with ?np.sum.
The file usually contains the categories: Parameters, Returns, See Also, Notes and Examples.
After the general description follows the syntax of the command. This usually indicates which (optional) arguments the command allows. Missing values are denoted by np.nan (“not a number”). If a vector contains missing values, np.sum() returns nan. The function np.nansum() ignores missing values.

x = np.array([1,2,np.nan,4,5])
print(x)
print(np.sum(x))
print(np.nansum(x))

[ 1.  2. nan  4.  5.]
nan
12.0


Note that the behavior of pandas is different: Here, missing values are ignored by default (argument skipna=True).

pd.Series(x).sum()

np.float64(12.0)
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

title: 9  The First Steps in Python
text:
9.7 Python Packages
There are tons of Python packages that are useful for different aspects of data analysis. Some packages that you will use all the time are numpy (vectors and matrices), pandas (data frames), matplotlib and seaborn (plots), and scipy and statsmodels (statistics). You can install packages in the terminal with pip install packagename, or directly in the Positron console with %pip install packagename. In order to use the package type import packagename, or, with a short name, import packagename as short_name. The package has to be installed only once (per virtual environment), but you have to load the package with import every time you want to use it.
crumbs: 9  The First Steps in Python

text:

Exercise 1:

x = np.array([157, 158, 159, 160, 161, 162, 163, 164])

The np.arange() function can be used in more complex operations along with arithmetic operators, and variable names. Have a look at the following expressions, and write down what sequence you think they will generate. Then check with Python.

NumPy has several functions for rounding. Let’s start with floor, ceil, and trunc:

Below you will find a series of arguments (x), and results (y), that can be obtained by choosing one or more of the 3 functions above (e.g.y = np.floor(x)). Which of the above 3 functions could have been used in each case? First, choose your answer without using Python, then check with Python.
